caption: The planetary nebula EGB 6, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: The planetary nebula EGB 6 resembles a vast bubble in space. It was captured with the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope, which stands at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO).

Planetary nebulae, despite the name, are unrelated to planets. They arise in the final millennia of intermediate-mass stars, those with between one and eight times the Sun's mass. Near the end of its life such a star becomes a red giant, as fusion temporarily reignites in its core. Layers of gas shed during that phase soak up huge amounts of energy and glow as a planetary nebula.

Those 'dying millennia' last only about 20,000 years. That is a mere blink compared with the lives of these stars, which shine steadily for between 30 million and 10 billion years, with heavier stars at the shorter end.
explore: The image was taken through filters for oxygen ([O III]) and hydrogen-alpha, and processed by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab. EGB 6 lies in the direction of Leo.

caption: The dwarf galaxy Sextans A, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Bright young stars glitter across Sextans A, an irregular dwarf galaxy whose roughly square outline stands out in this image from Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. It lies around 4.4 million light-years from Earth.
That odd outline has been twisted into shape by successive waves of supernova explosions. Sextans A is only a fraction of the Milky Way's size, measuring just about 5000 light-years across.

Irregular galaxies lack the orderly look of spirals or ellipticals and come in all sorts of strange shapes. They are relatively small, and they are often vulnerable to being pulled out of shape by close encounters or collisions with larger galaxies, which can sometimes explain their irregular forms. For Sextans A, the shaping is attributed to its own exploding stars. Bright young stars, like the ones sparkling here, are a sign that the galaxy is still forming new generations.
explore: The data were obtained and processed by P. Massey of Lowell Observatory with G. Jacoby, K. Olsen and C. Smith of AURA/NSF. Image processing was by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The dark nebula LDN 1622, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Shadowy clouds spread across this image of LDN 1622, a dark nebula. Dense clouds of gas and dust like this blot out the light of objects behind them, so they appear as ink-dark shapes against a backdrop of stars.

At a distance of 1300 light-years, LDN 1622 belongs to the nearby Orion complex, a star-forming area crowded with young stars and other dark nebulae. The picture was taken in 2018 with Mosaic-3, a wide-field camera on Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope in Arizona, built for covering large stretches of the night sky.

Mosaic-3 has since been retired to make room for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), described as the world's most powerful multi-object survey spectrograph. The swap shows one advantage of telescopes on the ground, which is that instruments can be upgraded or replaced as new technology arrives. This observation was made before the 2022 Contreras Fire, which affected Kitt Peak.
explore: The image credit names T. A. Rector, who also processed the image together with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab. It was made through g, i and hydrogen-alpha filters, and Kitt Peak is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The galaxy quartet NGC 6845, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: Four interacting galaxies share this view from Gemini South, all of them caught up in each other's gravity. The pair at the top are well-defined spiral galaxies, while the two below them are disk-shaped lenticular galaxies. Together they are known as NGC 6845, roughly 270 million light-years from Earth.

They sit in the constellation Telescopium, fittingly, one of a handful of constellations that honour scientific instruments instead of animals or figures from mythology. Between the galaxies are signs of star-forming regions and filaments of stars that have been pulled away from the galaxies they started in.

Because they are relatively close neighbours, the galaxies are interacting, and their mutual gravity is subtly distorting them. Astronomers believe the two spirals will eventually evolve into lenticular galaxies. A lenticular galaxy is a disk galaxy without prominent spiral arms, often with little ongoing star formation.
explore: Gemini South and its twin make up the International Gemini Observatory, run by NSF NOIRLab. The credit names G. Gimeno, R. J. Díaz and H. Dottori, with image processing by T.A. Rector, M. Zamani and D. de Martin.

caption: The young stellar jet MHO 1502, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: A knotted jet of gas stretches through this infrared image of MHO 1502, a young stellar jet captured from Chile by the international Gemini Observatory. The jet is embedded in an H II region, an area of star formation where hydrogen gas is lit up by young stars, in the direction of Vela.

The jet is bipolar, streaming out in two opposite directions, and it is made of a chain of knots. That pattern suggests its source, which is thought to be a pair of stars, has been emitting material in fits and starts rather than steadily, with each knot perhaps marking a separate outburst.

The crisp detail comes from Gemini South's adaptive optics system, which helps counteract the blurring caused by turbulence in Earth's atmosphere. Young stars often launch jets like this while they are still growing, and the jets can carry material far out into the surrounding cloud. The object listing also includes DGL 4.
explore: The observations were led by principal investigator L. Ferrero of the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba. Image processing was by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab. The Gemini Observatory is a Program of NSF's NOIRLab.

caption: The dark nebula TGU H1674, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: An inky-black cloud blots out the stars in this view of the dark nebula TGU H1674, in the direction of Vela. Dark nebulae, also called absorption nebulae, are clouds of gas and dust so dense that they block visible light, leaving them black against the starry background.

The dust grains inside such clouds absorb and scatter the light of stars behind them. Dark nebulae are often cold and dense enough that new stars can form within them, hidden from view at visible wavelengths until they clear away their surroundings.

TGU H1674 is one of many objects found within a large 1.3-gigapixel image of the Vela Supernova Remnant. That image was captured with the Dark Energy Camera, which the Department of Energy fabricated, on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. Its filters isolate light from oxygen, from sulfur, and from hydrogen-alpha combined with nitrogen.
explore: The Blanco telescope stands at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. Image processing was by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 289, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: Bluish spiral arms reach across space in this view of NGC 289, a large, extended spiral galaxy in the constellation Sculptor. It lies around 75 million light-years away, yet its arms span more than 100,000 light-years, making it larger than our own Milky Way.

NGC 289 is classified as a Type II Seyfert galaxy, with rich patches of star formation and a bright core, but overall it is relatively faint. Studies have found that it holds large amounts of dark matter, a common trait of galaxies with low surface brightness. Surface brightness describes how much light a galaxy gives off for each patch of sky it covers, so faint, spread-out galaxies score low.

Dark matter has never been directly observed. Astronomers infer it from its gravitational pull on stars and gas. The image comes from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), mounted on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. The camera has been open to other scientists since its original survey ended.
explore: The Blanco telescope stands at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), which is part of NSF NOIRLab. Image processing was by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage, J. Miller of Gemini Observatory and M. Zamani of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The Raspberry Nebula, LBN 867, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A characteristic red bloom of glowing gas marks this image of LBN 867, nicknamed the Raspberry Nebula, in the constellation Orion. The star HD 34989 shines prominently near the centre, wrapped in a subtle bluish glow.

Despite the nickname, the nebula is layered more like an onion than a raspberry, combining three objects in one. The red bloom is an emission nebula, glowing because light from HD 34989 ionizes its hydrogen gas. HD 34989 itself is a main sequence star. Prominent as it looks here, from Earth it appears only about as bright as the planet Uranus.

The third object is easy to miss. The faint bluish glow around the star is the reflection nebula vdB 38, where nearby interstellar dust bounces the star's blue-white light toward us. The image was captured by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope fitted with the Mosaic-3 detector, at Kitt Peak National Observatory, part of NSF NOIRLab.
explore: Main sequence stars are those steadily fusing hydrogen in their cores, the long, stable stage of a star's life that the Sun is in today. The credit and image processing are by T.A. Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage, with M. Zamani and D. de Martin of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3198, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 3198 appears in full in this image, from its bright central bulge out to the faint edges of its tightly wound arms. The galaxy sits in the constellation Ursa Major, about 47 million light-years away.

Almost everything in the background is a galaxy or galaxy cluster, a sea of distant galaxies in every shape, size and orientation. NGC 3198 itself has helped astronomers with the old problem of measuring distances accurately. Working out how far away anything is, from the Sun to remote galaxies, takes a combination of measurements and methods.

NGC 3198 allowed astronomers to calibrate distance measurements based on Cepheid variables, a type of pulsating star. Cepheids brighten and dim with a period linked to their true brightness, so comparing how bright one really is with how bright it appears reveals its distance. The Mosaic camera on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory recorded the galaxy.
explore: The observations were led by principal investigator M. T. Patterson of New Mexico State University, and the image was processed by Travis Rector, Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Kitt Peak is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The galaxy pair NGC 4411a and NGC 4411b with RSCG 55, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
story: Two spiral galaxies swirl through this small section of one of the First Look images captured by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Although NGC 4411b, on the left, and NGC 4411a, on the right, appear side by side, they show no signs of interacting, such as distorted arms.

Higher up in the frame sits RSCG 55, a group of galaxies that are interacting, linked by trails of material. Those trails are made of stars, gas and dust pulled from one galaxy to another during an earlier close encounter.

Galaxies that appear next to each other on the sky are not necessarily close in space, and one may lie far behind the other along the same line of sight. Distorted arms, bridges and tails are the telltale signs astronomers look for when judging whether galaxies are really interacting. This view was taken with the LSST Camera on Rubin's Simonyi Survey Telescope, looking toward the constellation Virgo.

caption: The galaxies NGC 1532 and NGC 1531, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1532, also known as Haley's Coronet, is locked in a one-sided tug of war with a smaller neighbour, the dwarf galaxy NGC 1531, in this view from the Dark Energy Camera. The pair lie about 55 million light-years away in the direction of Eridanus.

The image captures the pull each galaxy exerts on the other as a massive galaxy and a dwarf galaxy move toward a merger. The contest is uneven, since the larger galaxy's gravity dominates, but the dwarf still leaves its mark, because interactions like this can distort a spiral's arms and stir up star formation.

Encounters between a large galaxy and a dwarf companion are thought to be one way big galaxies grow over time. The picture was taken with the US Department of Energy's Dark Energy Camera (DECam), which works on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, located at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile.

caption: The Silver Sliver Galaxy, NGC 891, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: A spiral galaxy seen almost perfectly edge-on stretches across this image as a long, thin sliver. This is NGC 891, nicknamed the Silver Sliver Galaxy, captured with the Mosaic instrument on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. Viewed this way, it closely resembles our own Milky Way as we see it from Earth.

Its edge-on angle makes NGC 891 a good place to test the galactic fountain model. In that model, stellar winds and supernovae in a galaxy's disk blast gas out into the surrounding space. Some of that gas can condense and rain back down onto the disk, where it becomes fresh fuel for new stars. Seeing a disk side-on makes gas above and below it easier to spot.

The frame is also crowded with other objects near and far. Bright foreground stars in our own galaxy intrude on the view, while distant galaxies lurk in the background. NGC 891 lies in the direction of the constellation Andromeda.
explore: The observations were led by principal investigator M.T. Patterson of New Mexico State University, and the image was processed by Travis Rector, Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Kitt Peak is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The barred lenticular galaxy NGC 7020, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
story: In this Gemini South image, the centre of NGC 7020 has a subtle but unmistakable six-sided shape. NGC 7020 is a barred lenticular galaxy in Pavo, a constellation of the southern sky. Flanking the hexagon to the left and right are two denser clumps of stars, called ansae.

A hexagon is an uncommon shape for any object in space, and rarer still for a whole galaxy. To build one, a large number of stars must follow orbits confined to a very narrow band, and the ansae are part of that orbital path. The unusual shape seems to come from a very rare orbital resonance, or from some phenomenon not yet understood. An orbital resonance happens when orbits fall into a regular, repeating relationship, which can herd objects into distinct patterns.
The 8-meter Gemini South telescope stands on Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes. Together with its partner, Gemini North in Hawai‘i, it gives astronomers a deep view of the whole night sky.
explore: The credit names H. Dottori, R. J. Díaz and G. Gimeno, with image processing by T.A. Rector, M. Zamani and D. de Martin. The International Gemini Observatory is a Program of NSF NOIRLab, and the image used g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters.

caption: The emission nebula RCW 120, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
story: A crimson cloud glows in this view of RCW 120, also called Sharpless 2-3, an emission nebula and star-forming region in the constellation Scorpius. Dark lanes wind through the red gas.

The red colour comes from ionized hydrogen. Intense heat from young, massive stars inside the nebula energizes the gas, which then gives off light at deep red and infrared wavelengths. The dark lanes are made of the same material but are less energized, so they do not glow.

Emission nebulae often contain bright stars, and such stars build up many heavier elements, silicon and iron among them, by fusing lighter ones together. RCW 120 also shelters an unusual star still in its embryonic stage, which astronomers expect to grow into one of the Milky Way's brightest. The view comes from the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3981, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: The outstretched arms of NGC 3981 seem to dissolve into space in this image. At the centre of this unbarred spiral galaxy, about 65 million light-years away in the constellation Crater, is a bright core that hosts a supermassive black hole, ringed by a disk of hot, young stars. Streams of dust thread through the spiral arms, along with further young stars.

The arms' irregular, stretched-out shape is probably the result of gravitational pull during an encounter with one of the galaxy's neighbours. NGC 3981 belongs to the NGC 4038 Group, which also includes the well-known interacting Antennae Galaxies.

That group, in turn, forms a small piece of the Virgo Supercluster, a vast assembly of galaxies to which the Milky Way also belongs. The picture was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), built by the Department of Energy, working on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2541, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Spiral arms wind around NGC 2541 in fine detail in this image from Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. It is classified as an unbarred spiral galaxy, with sweeping spiral arms but none of the central bar-shaped structure seen in galaxies such as the Milky Way.

At a distance of 37 million light-years, NGC 2541 sits in Lynx, a constellation squeezed in among Ursa Major, Gemini and Leo. Lynx was one of 10 constellations newly introduced in the 17th century by the astronomer Johannes Hevelius.

Because its stars are so dim, Hevelius said that only the lynx-eyed, meaning people with unusually sharp vision, could ever find it. Astronomers sort galaxies into a variety of types, and whether a spiral has a central bar is one of the features they use to classify it.
explore: The observations were led by principal investigator M. T. Patterson of New Mexico State University, and the image was processed by Travis Rector, Mahdi Zamani and Davide de Martin. Kitt Peak is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: Two galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
story: This close-up from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory focuses on two galaxies that belong to the Virgo Cluster. The object listing for the image includes M61.

While Rubin was observing this part of the sky, it caught a plethora of asteroids zipping across the field. They left tiny streaks, which have been removed from this version of the picture. A second version keeps them, so viewers can blink between the two and spot the moving objects.

Asteroids are rocky bodies orbiting the Sun. Because they move against the background of distant stars and galaxies, they land in a slightly different position in each exposure, which is how a survey telescope can pick them out. A galaxy cluster, like Virgo, is a large gathering of galaxies held together by gravity. This view was taken with the LSST Camera on Rubin's Simonyi Survey Telescope, through u, g, r and i filters, combining several exposures.

caption: The Pleiades star cluster and surroundings, imaged by the Digitized Sky Survey
story: This colour image shows the Pleiades star cluster and the region around it, in the constellation Taurus. A yellow arrow marks the position of the star HD 23514, and an inset of artwork sits in the lower right corner.

HD 23514 is singled out because, according to the release title, astronomers spotted evidence there for colliding planet embryos, the building blocks from which planets are thought to grow. The Pleiades itself is an open star cluster, a group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas and dust.

Inseok Song, of the Spitzer Science Center, made the picture by merging B-, R- and I-band images taken from the second-generation Digitized Sky Survey, displayed as blue, green and red respectively. The inset is artwork credited to Gemini Observatory and Lynette Cook, not a photograph, so only the main image shows the real sky.

caption: The triple star system HP Tau, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
story: Three stars sit at the centre of this image, wrapped in a large arcing reflection nebula. They form a triple star system that includes HP Tau, a variable star in Taurus that lies more than 550 light-years away.

HP Tau belongs to the T Tauri class of young, unruly stars that are easing into a calmer phase of life called the main sequence. How long a star stays on the main sequence depends on its mass. The Sun, for example, is about halfway through its main-sequence lifetime of roughly 10 billion years.

The surrounding nebula shines by reflection rather than emission. Its dust reflects light from nearby stars instead of glowing on its own, the way emission nebulae elsewhere in the Universe do. The image was made from data gathered by Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope.

caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4261 and neighbours, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
story: A trail of galaxies and stars runs through this small section of one of the First Look images from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Dominating the upper half is NGC 4261, a large elliptical galaxy, while the lenticular galaxy NGC 4281 sits at the bottom left.

Between and around them lies a crowd of other galaxies and stars. NGC 4261 is about 100 million light-years away, in the direction of Virgo. Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of stars with little gas and few newly forming stars, while lenticular galaxies have a disk like a spiral but lack prominent spiral arms.

The view was captured with the LSST Camera on Rubin's Simonyi Survey Telescope, combining exposures through u, g, r and i filters. Stacking many exposures lets faint galaxies emerge that a single short look would miss, helping to bring out the many objects between and around the two big galaxies.

caption: The reflection nebula NGC 2170, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
story: Bright swathes of colour streak across this image of the reflection nebula NGC 2170. Dust grains bounce back blue light from hot stars buried inside the nebula, warm hydrogen gas glows deep red, and dark tendrils of dust absorb the light of stars and gas behind them.

In a reflection nebula, diffuse clouds of interstellar dust scatter the light of nearby stars toward us. Blue light is scattered more readily than red, which is one reason reflection nebulae often look blue. In NGC 2170 that blue mixes with the red glow of hydrogen and the dark threads of dust, so three different effects share one scene.

NGC 2170 belongs to Monoceros, the Unicorn, a dim constellation that straddles the celestial equator. The observations were made with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile.

caption: The reflection nebula NGC 2626, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
story: NGC 2626 looks vivid enough to pass for a painting, but this is a real picture of the reflection nebula, which lies in the direction of Vela, 3300 light-years from Earth. Red patches of nebulosity within it are glowing hydrogen gas.

A reflection nebula gives off no light of its own. Instead, its dust particles scatter light from one or more nearby stars back toward us. Blue light scatters more efficiently than red, so reflection nebulae often take on a bluish tint.

That is the same physics that turns Earth's daytime sky blue, as sunlight scatters in our atmosphere. The observations behind this image were made with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), part of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: Mauna Loa's lava glow and a lava light pillar, seen from Maunakea, Hawaiʻi
story: The reddish glow of Mauna Loa's lava flows appears in this night view, recorded by a Cloudcam belonging to the International Gemini Observatory. The camera sits close to Maunakea's snowy summit, which is the highest point in the frame. The camera runs around the clock. Also visible is an exceptionally rare lava light pillar.

Mauna Loa, a volcano on the island of Hawaiʻi, started erupting on 27 November 2022, as lava broke out of fissures in Moku‘āweoweo, the caldera at its summit. Described as the world's largest active volcano, it had not erupted in nearly 40 years, and the glow of its flows could be seen across the island. The picture was taken at 02:15 local time on 29 November.

Light pillars are more often seen with the Sun. A lava pillar needs a rare combination of an erupting volcano to provide light near the horizon, high-altitude cloud and freezing temperatures. Together these produce millions of ice crystals floating horizontally, which reflect the light toward the observer.
explore: Staff at Gemini North and the other Maunakea Observatories watched closely as flows moved down Mauna Loa's flank toward the Daniel K. Inouye Highway (Saddle Road). On Mauna Loa itself, lava crossed the access road to NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory and cut its power, though the eruption posed no threat to the Maunakea observatories.

caption: The planetary nebula PN M 2-53, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
story: PN M 2-53 looks like an inky patch of space smudged by a giant thumbprint. The planetary nebula lies about 12000 light-years away in the direction of Lacerta and was captured by Gemini North, one of the international Gemini Observatory's two telescopes.

The name 'planetary nebula' is thoroughly misleading, because these objects have nothing to do with planets, or even with exoplanets. The term goes back to the late 1700s, when astronomers thought the glowing gas shapes looked like planets. Wrong as it is, the name has stuck.

In reality, planetary nebulae come from some dying stars at the very end of their lives. The stars shed layers of gas and dust, which are then lit up by the cores left behind. This image was made through filters for oxygen, sulfur and hydrogen-alpha, each capturing the glow of a particular gas in the shell.
explore: The observations were led by principal investigator Rafael Andrés Pignata of the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba. Image processing was by T. A. Rector, J. Miller, M. Zamani and D. de Martin, and the Gemini Observatory is a Program of NSF NOIRLab.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4519, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
story: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4519 features in this small section of one of the First Look images from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Directly above it sits its companion, a lenticular galaxy called PGC 41706. NGC 4519 lies about 55 million light-years away, in the direction of Virgo.

A barred spiral has a straight bar of stars running through its centre, with spiral arms winding out from the ends of the bar. A lenticular galaxy has a disk like a spiral but lacks prominent arms. Neighbouring galaxies like these can influence each other through gravity over long periods, tugging on stars and gas.

This view comes from Rubin's LSST Camera on the Simonyi Survey Telescope, which combined exposures through u, g, r and i filters. Stacking many exposures reveals faint detail that a single short look would miss.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy IC 4212, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
story: This image shows IC 4212, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Virgo. It sits close to the celestial equator, so at certain times of year it can be seen, at least partly, from both hemispheres.

The celestial equator is the projection of Earth's equator onto the sky. Objects near it rise and set for observers both north and south of the equator, unlike objects near the celestial poles, which can only be seen from one hemisphere.

A barred spiral galaxy has a straight bar of stars across its centre, with spiral arms extending from the ends of the bar. Bars are thought to help funnel gas toward a galaxy's centre, where it can feed new star formation. The image was taken with the Dark Energy Camera on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope, through g, r and z filters, as part of observations led by J. Moustakas of Siena College.

caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-42, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
story: This view shows Sh2-42, a planetary nebula in the constellation Sagittarius. It was captured with the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.

Despite the name, planetary nebulae are unrelated to planets. NOIRLab likens them to funeral pyres, made by red giant stars as their lives draw to a close. As such a giant swells, it casts its outer layers of gas into space. The hot core left exposed then ionizes the surrounding material, making it glow in a range of vivid colours.

The Sun, too, is expected to produce a planetary nebula as it nears the end of its life, but not for another 5 billion years. The colours in images like this trace different gases. Hydrogen-alpha and oxygen ([O III]) filters were among those used here, each picking out light given off by a specific element.

caption: The Milky Way and zodiacal light over Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, Chile
story: Two bands of light rise side by side from the horizon above Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. One is an arm of our Milky Way, and the other, to its right, is the fainter glow of zodiacal light.

The Milky Way's glow comes from unresolved stars and other material, interrupted here and there by dark patches of dust and gas. Zodiacal light is sunlight bouncing off interplanetary dust, debris that remains from the time the Solar System formed. Because most of that dust lies in the plane the planets travel, the ecliptic, the zodiacal light traces it. Planets inside the glow confirm the line. Climbing upward from the horizon, they are Jupiter, Venus, Mars and Saturn.

The Milky Way arm appears between the DIMM1 Seeing Monitor and the decommissioned CHilean Automatic Supernova sEarch (CHASE). Other telescopes in the scene, from left to right, are the US Naval Observatory Deep South Telescope, the DIMM2 Seeing Monitor, aTmCam and the SMARTS 1.0-meter telescope.
explore: CTIO, a Program of NSF NOIRLab, sits in a high, dry, remote mountain setting in Chile, where sensitive equipment can pick up subtle light in the night sky. The photo was taken during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition by Tomáš Slovinský, a NOIRLab Audiovisual Ambassador.

understand.eye: The caption gives no exposure details, but long camera exposures generally gather more light than the eye, making faint glows like zodiacal light easier to see in photographs.
